text: Chapter Five covered mapping data flows — visual, Spark-based transformations inside classic ADF. Fabric's equivalent is Dataflow Gen2, and the single most important thing to understand is that it's genuinely not the same engine wearing a different name. Dataflow Gen2 is built on Power Query — the same engine behind Excel's Get and Transform and Power BI dataflows — not Spark.

If you've ever used Power Query in Excel or Power BI, this editor is immediately familiar: Applied Steps, column quality indicators, the same ribbon-driven transformation experience. That familiarity is genuinely deliberate — Power BI report authors already comfortable with Power Query can be productive in Dataflow Gen2 almost immediately, a different audience than Spark-literate engineers typically required for mapping data flows.

Where a classic Power BI dataflow only ever stored data in its own internal storage, Dataflow Gen2 writes to a genuinely wide set of real external destinations — including two Fabric-native options, Lakehouse Tables and Warehouse, that simply didn't exist as connector types in classic mapping data flows at all. Load into a Lakehouse, then hand straight off to a Spark notebook, all sharing the same OneLake storage.

Neither engine is strictly better — they're built for genuinely different transformation styles. A wrangling, exploratory, column-by-column cleanup task fits Dataflow Gen2's Power Query model naturally. A heavy, large-scale join-and-aggregate transformation across huge datasets still leans on Spark's real strengths — exactly what mapping data flows, and Fabric's own Spark notebooks, are built for.

Same underlying idea as Chapter Five, a genuinely different engine and a genuinely different audience. Next: Pipelines in Fabric — the same orchestration model you already know, with several real building blocks that work differently underneath.
